modules.title: The Unified Mathematical Spine
modules.summary: Welcome to the Mathematical Maturity Engine. I'm your instructor, and this first module is the whole reason this course exists: the unified mathematical spine — college algebra through probability and statistics, in the verified course order. We climb it together: equations and functions, trigonometry and the unit circle, precalculus (complex numbers, vectors, the limits preview), calculus I (limits, derivatives, integrals, the Fundamental Theorem), calculus II (integration techniques, series, Taylor), discrete mathematics (logic, proofs, combinatorics, graphs), linear algebra (eigenvalues, least squares, SVD, matrix calculus for ML), and probability and statistics (distributions, Bayes and MLE/MAP, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, regression, hypothesis testing). I gate every node at mastery: no calculus without functions, no machine learning without linear algebra.
objectives: Solve equations and work functions fluently: composition, inverses, graphs.
Differentiate and integrate: rules, applications, the Fundamental Theorem.
Prove: induction, contradiction, invariants — discrete math as a writing discipline.
Diagonalize: eigenvalues, SVD, least squares — linear algebra for ML.
Reason under uncertainty: Bayes, MLE, CLT, regression, testing.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Function** — a rule assigning each input exactly one output; the core object of algebra — domain, range, composition, inverses.
- **Exponential and logarithm** — an inverse pair, the growth/decay language; change of base: log_a(b) = ln b / ln a.
- **Unit circle** — x²+y²=1; every trigonometric identity lives here.
- **Complex number** — a+bi, the algebraic closure: every polynomial equation has its solutions here.
- **Limit** — the value a function approaches; continuity and the derivative both rest on the epsilon-delta idea.
- **Derivative** — the instantaneous rate of change; definition → rules → the chain rule.
- **Chain rule** — (f∘g)′ = f′(g(x))·g′(x); the whole game in disguise — backprop is the chain rule at scale.
- **Integral** — accumulated area; the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums.
- **Fundamental Theorem** — differentiation and integration are inverses: ∫ₐᵇ f′ = f(b)−f(a).
- **Series** — an infinite sum; convergence decided by tests — p-series (converges iff p>1), ratio, comparison.
- **Taylor series** — the local polynomial approximation f(x) ≈ Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!; bound the error with the Lagrange remainder.
- **Induction** — proof by domino: base case → hypothesis → step.
- **Proof by contradiction** — assume the negation, derive the absurd; the contrapositive rides alongside.
- **Pigeonhole principle** — n+1 items in n boxes forces a box with two or more; deceptively powerful.
- **Combinatorics** — organized counting: every 'how many' reduces to product rule, sum rule, and choose.
- **Graph** — vertices and edges; the universal model — paths, cycles, trees, coloring, Euler/Hamilton. When stuck, draw the graph.
- **Modular arithmetic** — arithmetic on remainders; the road to RSA.
- **Finite automaton** — the simplest computation model; the preview of theory.
- **Eigenvalue/eigenvector** — the scalar λ and direction v with Av = λv: where the matrix acts by pure scaling — PCA, PageRank, quantum states.
- **Least squares** — the projection of the data onto the model space; the geometry of regression.
- **SVD** — A = UΣVᵀ, the everything-decomposition: rank, compression, latent factors.
- **Matrix calculus** — gradients of vector-valued functions; the language ML optimizers speak.
- **Distribution** — the zoo: normal, binomial, Poisson, exponential; know each one's story.
- **Bayes' theorem** — P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E); the update rule for all reasoning under uncertainty.
- **MLE/MAP** — fit by maximizing likelihood (MLE), or likelihood × prior (MAP).
- **Law of large numbers** — sample averages converge to the expectation; frequencies become probabilities.
- **Central limit theorem** — sums of many small independent effects go normal; the reason normal distributions are everywhere.
- **Regression and hypothesis testing** — fit the model, then ask whether the fit means anything; p-values and confidence intervals — and their misuses.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
We estimate sin(0.5) with a Taylor polynomial — then prove how wrong we are allowed to be. This is the estimation discipline the whole spine trains.
1. **Write the polynomial.** sin x at a=0: P₅(x) = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! = x − x³/6 + x⁵/120.
2. **Evaluate at x = 0.5.** x³ = 0.125, x⁵ = 0.03125, so P₅(0.5) = 0.5 − 0.0208333 + 0.0002604 ≈ 0.4794271.
3. **Compute the true value and the error.** sin(0.5) = 0.4794255, so the actual error is ≈ 1.54e-06.
4. **Bound the error before trusting it.** The Lagrange remainder after degree 5 is bounded by the next term's magnitude: |x|⁷/7! = 0.5⁷/5040 ≈ 1.55e-06. The true error sits under the bound — this is estimation with a guarantee.
5. **Read the lesson.** Three terms buy six correct digits at x = 0.5, and the remainder tells you what the next term is worth before you compute it. Approximation with guarantees is the whole of applied analysis — and the fluency gate here is real: differentiate and integrate the standard forms without pausing.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Your capstone: **The Spine Map**. Pick a destination — an IL-07 machine-learning module, the electrician aptitude battery, or the quant ladder in this course's fourth module. Trace its prerequisite chain back to arithmetic: list every spine node the destination depends on (ML needs gradients → derivatives → limits → functions; SVD → eigenvalues → matrix algebra; Bayes → distributions → probability). For each node, solve one problem drawn from this module's quizzes or the Taylor / Monte Carlo / least-squares script labs, and write out one proof (induction of your choice, or the epsilon-delta argument for a limit). Deliverable: a one-page prerequisite map — nodes, edges, and your honest mastery self-score per node — plus a two-week remediation plan for your weakest node with daily 15-minute drills. Grading rule: the map must name every dependency honestly. If you cannot derive it, the node is red. This module gates IL-03's algorithms and IL-08's theory — no induction, no algorithms.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery — and honesty. What this module does NOT do: it does not certify you in anything (Interstitium Labs confers no certificate — see the course honesty note), and reading it once does not make you fluent; the script labs and the weekly proof are where fluency forms. Noah asks things like:
- State the chain rule and name one place it appears outside a calculus class.
- In one paragraph each: why no machine learning without linear algebra, and why no machine learning without probability.
- Show Noah your spine-map's red nodes and the remediation plan — 'I read it' is not mastery.

(f∘g)' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Backprop is the chain rule at scale.
Differentiation and integration are inverses: ∫ₐᵇ f' = f(b)−f(a).
Local polynomial approximation: f(x) ≈ Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!. Bound error with Lagrange remainder.
Base → hypothesis → step. The domino principle.
n+1 items in n boxes → some box has 2+. Deceptively powerful.
Av = λv — the direction the matrix only scales.
A = UΣVᵀ — rank, compression, latent factors in one factorization.

modules.title: Tech Math: Trade-Applied Mathematics
modules.summary: Welcome back — I'm your instructor, and this module trades the classroom for the shop: tech math, trade-applied mathematics. We drill whole-number operations and fractions, decimals, and percents until they're reflexes — no calculators on aptitude tests — then measurement in both US customary and metric, reading tape, calipers, and micrometers to the instrument's precision, with dimensional analysis on every conversion: units cancel like fractions. Then shop math: ratio and proportion, percent applications (markup, waste, discount), area and volume estimation from drawings, and reading scales. We finish with the readiness verification: a timed run against the aptitude battery with gap diagnosis — diagnostic, not judgmental.
objectives: Compute fractions, decimals, percents fluently — under time.
Convert units with dimensional analysis; read instruments to their precision.
Estimate materials: area, volume, waste factors from drawings.
Verify readiness against the aptitude battery; diagnose gaps.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Fraction** — a ratio of integers; fluency means adding unlike denominators and multiplying straight across without a calculator.
- **Percent** — parts per hundred; part = percent × whole — the single formula behind markup, discount, and waste. Instant conversions are the fluency bar: 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%.
- **Estimation** — an order-of-magnitude check before precise computation; Fermi-style: is it 10 or 100? Estimation first, calculation second — catch the decimal error before it costs material.
- **Dimensional analysis** — treating units as algebraic quantities that cancel like fractions: ft × 12 in/ft = in. Write every conversion as a fraction and let the units guide the arithmetic.
- **Tolerance** — the drawing's ± band (e.g., ±1/16″); the pass/fail law, not a suggestion. Measure to decide pass/fail, not from curiosity.
- **Precision** — how finely an instrument reads; read to the instrument's precision, never beyond it.
- **Waste factor** — the allowance for offcuts and error: order = net × (1 + waste%) — 10% for simple cuts, 15%+ for complex ones.
- **Scale** — the drawing-to-reality ratio (e.g., 1/4″ = 1′); measure the drawing, multiply by the scale — and verify against a known dimension.
- **Ratio and proportion** — relative quantities in the shop: mix ratios, gear ratios; solve by scaling to the total parts.
- **The bridge constant** — 25.4 mm = 1 inch, exactly; the constant that joins the two measurement systems.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
We estimate material for a job from a drawing — the exact sequence a tradesperson runs before ordering. Follow it on your own room.
1. **Read the drawing.** Confirm the scale (e.g., 1/4″ = 1′) and note every tolerance callout — the ± is the law.
2. **Measure on paper, scale to reality.** Measure each dimension on the drawing, multiply by the scale factor — then verify against one printed known dimension. If 3.5″ on a 1/4″=1′ drawing, that's 14 feet real.
3. **Compute the net quantity.** A 20′ × 12′ floor is 240 sq ft net. Write the units as fractions so they cancel.
4. **Apply the waste factor.** Simple layout: order = net × (1 + waste%) = 240 × 1.10 = 264 sq ft. Complex cuts: use 15%+.
5. **Convert units with dimensional analysis.** Flooring sells by the square yard: 264 sq ft × (1 sq yd / 9 sq ft) = 29.33… → order 30 sq yd. Units guide the arithmetic — if they don't cancel to sq yd, the setup is wrong.
6. **Sanity-check by estimation first.** Your estimate said 'about 30'; if the arithmetic had said 264, the decimal is wrong — trust the estimate's order of magnitude. Estimation first, calculation second.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Your capstone: **The Contractor's Bid**. Measure a real room — or work from a one-room flooring drawing — and produce a materials estimate end to end: real dimensions from the scale, net area or volume, waste factor applied (state your percentage and why), unit conversions with the dimensional-analysis chain written out, and one percent application (a discount or markup) computed with the part = percent × whole formula. Deliverable: a one-page estimate sheet plus a two-minute timed fraction/percent self-test with your score and the problems that slowed you down — that list is your drill backlog. Grading rule: every number on the sheet must show its units cancelling; a number without units is a guess.

notes.body:

- Convert 5/8 to a decimal and a percent, under ten seconds.
- Explain why estimation comes before calculation — and what a missed order of magnitude costs on a real job.
- A drawing at 1/4″ = 1′ shows 3.5″ for a wall. How long is the wall, and how do you verify?

modules.title: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance
modules.summary: Welcome to the electrician apprenticeship track — I'm your instructor, and this module is your entry ramp into the electrical training ALLIANCE pipeline. We walk the interim credential sequence in order — Constructing Your Future, Electrical Job Information 1, Applied Codeology 2023, Electrical Theory 1 (DC), Construction Drawings — because sequence matters: each unlocks the next. You will learn SQ3R technical reading (survey, question, read, recite, review), because in the trades you read to perform, not to recall. We cover workplace conduct and well-being, apprentice-wage budgeting and credit, code literacy — finding articles under time, reading 'shall' versus 'shall be permitted', never assuming an exception — and the algebra fringe the aptitude batteries actually test: fractions through functions, number series.
objectives: Complete the interim credential sequence in order.
Read technically with SQ3R: survey → question → read → recite → review.
Navigate code articles: organization, 'shall' language, exceptions.
Pass the algebra fringe: fractions through functions, number series.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **SQ3R** — Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review; technical reading as reading to perform — the test is doing, not recalling. Recite from memory: recognition is not recall.
- **Ohm's law** — V = IR; voltage drives current through resistance. The physics under everything electrical.
- **Power** — P = VI; with V = IR, the DC trinity.
- **Series circuit** — one path for current; resistances add directly: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ….
- **Parallel circuit** — voltage is common across branches; reciprocal resistances add: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
- **'Shall'** — mandatory language in code. Misreading it fails inspections.
- **'Shall be permitted'** — permissive language: allowed, not required. The language of law — 'shall' = must, 'shall be permitted' = may.
- **Exception** — a code carve-out that is never assumed; read the specific exception — it doesn't transfer to other articles.
- **Construction drawings** — symbols, schedules, one-lines; read them to build.
- **Workplace conduct** — standards, reporting channels, bystander responsibility: the trade's social contract.
- **Apprentice-wage planning** — the wage grows in steps; budget to the step you're on, plan for the next. Budget construction: income − obligations = reality.
- **Credit utilization** — the share of available credit in use; keep it under 30% — the fastest lever on the score.
- **Number series** — aptitude-test pattern finding: differences first, ratios second, alternation third.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Code literacy is a lookup skill, not a memory skill. Drill the timed article-finding procedure — the index is the map.
1. **State the question precisely.** 'Which article covers conductor ampacity?' — not 'something about wires.'
2. **Go to the index first.** Never browse chapters blind; the index maps keywords to articles.
3. **Index → chapter → article.** Read the article's scope paragraph before its subsections — scope tells you whether you're even in the right place.
4. **Read the language.** Distinguish 'shall' from 'shall be permitted' in every requirement; flag any exceptions and read them in full — exceptions are never assumed and never transfer.
5. **Time the lookup.** Record every miss and its cause: wrong keyword, skipped index, misread exception.
6. **Repeat with five articles** until lookups run under your target time. Practice the lookup, not just the reading.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Your capstone: **The Load Calc**. A mock small apartment: list its loads — lighting, receptacles, small appliances — and compute the total current on 120V circuits with the DC trinity (P = VI, rearranged). Size the conductors using the code's ampacity-table workflow: locate the tables with the timed lookup drill from 'Hands-on procedure', and document the full lookup path (index → chapter → article) for each table you used. Produce a one-page panel schedule: circuit, load, current, conductor size. Deliverable: the load table, the panel schedule, and the two articles you cited — each with the 'shall' language you found in it. Grading rule: no article number from memory — every citation must show its lookup path.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery — and honesty. What this module does NOT do: the interim credentials are real programs run by real organizations — this module does not enroll you in them or confer them; confirm current requirements with the organizations. Code-literacy practice here does not replace the codebook, and the aptitude drills are practice, not the battery. Noah asks things like:
- State Ohm's law from memory, then solve: 12V across 4Ω in series with 2Ω — what current?
- Explain the difference between 'shall' and 'shall be permitted' — and why misreading it fails an inspection.
- Continue this number series aloud and name the pattern: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?

cards.back: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review — reading to perform.
VI. And V = IR. The DC trinity.
Shall = mandatory. Shall be permitted = allowed. The language of law.
Never assumed — read the specific exception; it doesn't transfer.
Under 30% — the fastest lever on the score.
42 — differences 4,6,8,10,12, so next is 30+12=42 (pattern n(n+1)).

100W × 5h = 500Wh = 0.5 kWh — see 'Concepts' on power.
Series resistances add: 60Ω — see 'Concepts'.
(100×100)/(100+100) = 50Ω — see 'Concepts' on parallel circuits.

quiz.explain: Permissive language — may, not must. See 'Concepts'.

modules.title: Quantitative Finance Mathematics
modules.summary: Welcome to the quant summit — I'm your instructor, and this module is the mathematical prerequisites beneath the quant ladder: nothing more, nothing less. We survey measure-theoretic probability — sigma-algebras, measures, random variables as measurable functions, expectation as integration, the convergence hierarchy — because that is the language the quant literature speaks. Then stochastic processes: Markov chains and their stationary distributions, queues with Little's law, Monte Carlo simulation, random walks and the Brownian motion preview. Finally the financial-math prerequisites: time value of money, returns with variance and covariance, the Black-Scholes prerequisites without hand-waving — know what each assumption buys — and discrete-time binomial pricing by replication.
objectives: State the measure-theoretic foundations: sigma-algebras, expectation as integration.
Analyze Markov chains: stationary distributions, absorption.
Price time: present value, returns, variance/covariance, discrete models.
Connect the math to Black-Scholes prerequisites without hand-waving.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Sigma-algebra** — a collection of events closed under complement and countable union: the events we can assign probability to.
- **Measure** — a nonnegative, countably additive set function; probability is a measure with total 1.
- **Random variable** — a measurable function X: Ω → ℝ; the grown-up view of a random quantity.
- **Expectation** — E[X] = ∫X dP: expectation as Lebesgue integral.
- **Convergence modes** — almost-sure ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution, plus Lᵖ; know the hierarchy and the implications.
- **Markov chain** — a memoryless stochastic process; the future depends only on the present state.
- **Stationary distribution** — π with πP = π and Σπ = 1: the chain's long-run behavior; solve it, don't guess it.
- **Queueing and Little's law** — M/M/1 basics; L = λW: the long-run average number in the system equals arrival rate times average time — deceptively deep.
- **Monte Carlo simulation** — when analysis fails, simulation answers, with confidence intervals; error shrinks as 1/√N.
- **Random walk** — the discrete-time ancestor of Brownian motion; scaling limits give the continuous-time intuition.
- **Brownian motion** — the continuous-time scaling limit of random walks; the noise engine of continuous finance models.
- **Present value** — PV = FV/(1+r)ᵗ: discounting — a dollar today is not a dollar tomorrow; the atom of finance math.
- **Returns, variance, covariance** — the statistics of portfolios; diversification as variance reduction, needing correlation below 1 — the almost-free lunch.
- **Binomial tree** — up/down moves with risk-neutral probabilities; price by replication and backward induction — the computable foundation beneath the continuous models.
- **Risk-neutral pricing** — price as if investors were risk-neutral; replication, not preferences, determines the price.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
We find a Markov chain's stationary distribution two ways: exactly, then by estimation — and compare. The chain: P = [[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]].
1. **Solve it exactly.** πP = π with π₀ + π₁ = 1 gives π₀ = 0.7π₀ + 0.4π₁ → π₀ = 4/7 ≈ 0.5714, π₁ = 3/7 ≈ 0.4286. That's the chain's long-run behavior, in closed form.
2. **Estimate it by simulation.** Run 100,000 transitions from state 0 and count the fraction of steps spent in state 0. Result: ≈ 0.5736 — the law of large numbers converging frequencies onto the stationary distribution.
3. **Compare.** The estimate lands within 0.0021 of 4/7 ≈ 0.5714. Estimation agrees with analysis.
4. **Read the lesson.** Simulation is estimation with a rate: error shrinks as 1/√N, so each extra decimal costs roughly 100× the samples. When analysis gives 4/7, you verify; when analysis fails, Monte Carlo answers — with confidence intervals.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Your capstone: **The Binomial Pricer**. Price a two-step European call with S₀ = 100, up factor u = 1.1, down factor d = 0.9, rate r = 5% per step, strike K = 100. Compute the risk-neutral probability p = (1+r−d)/(u−d) = 0.75; build the stock tree (up-up 121, up-down 99, down-down 81); write the terminal payoffs (21, 0, 0); work backward — the up-node value is 15.00, the down-node is 0.00 — to the root price of 10.71. Then show the replication portfolio at each node: Δ shares plus the bond position that reproduces the option's payoff. Deliverable: the tree diagram, the price, the replication table, and one paragraph stating what each Black-Scholes ingredient (lognormal prices, constant volatility, frictionless markets) assumes and what that assumption buys — no hand-waving. Grading rule: the replication table must balance at every node; an unbalanced hedge is a wrong price.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery — and honesty. What this module does NOT do: it is prerequisites, not trading — it does not teach you to trade, predict markets, or pass a quant interview on its own. Measure theory is surveyed here, not mastered; and the Black-Scholes ingredients assume constant volatility and frictionless markets, assumptions that fail in practice. Noah asks things like:
- State the convergence hierarchy: what does almost-sure convergence imply?
- Explain what risk-neutral pricing does NOT mean — and what actually determines the price.
- Compute the present value of $100 in 2 years at 5%, and say in one sentence what discounting means.

cards.back: Events we can measure: closed under complement and countable unions.
∫X dP — expectation as Lebesgue integral.
πP = π, Σπ = 1 — the chain's long-run behavior.
L = λW — average number = arrival rate × average time.
100/1.05² ≈ $90.70. Discounting.
Replication — risk-neutral probabilities, backward induction.

Solve πP=π with Σπ=1: π₀=4/7, π₁=3/7 — see 'Worked estimation'.
L = λW = 6 customers average — Little's law, see 'Concepts'.
Covariance < 1 → combined variance < weighted average — see 'Concepts'.
1000 × 1.06³ = $1,191.02 — see 'Concepts' on present value.

quiz.explain: No-arbitrage + replication — preferences drop out. See 'Concepts'.

scriptLabs.title: Taylor Approximation Laboratory
scriptLabs.brief: Approximate sin(x) with Taylor polynomials of degree 1, 3, 5, 7 at x=0.5; compute actual errors and the Lagrange bound. See convergence happen.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    # TODO: sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^k x^(2k+1) / (2k+1)!
    pass

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={abs(approx-math.sin(x)):.2e}')

scriptLabs.solution:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    return sum((-1)**k * x**(2*k+1) / math.factorial(2*k+1) for k in range(n+1))

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    err = abs(approx - math.sin(x))
    # Lagrange bound: |R| <= |x|^(2n+3)/(2n+3)!
    bound = abs(x)**(2*n+3) / math.factorial(2*n+3)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={err:.2e} bound={bound:.2e}')
# Lesson: error collapses as degree grows — approximation with guarantees.

    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} error={abs(est-math.pi):.2e}')
scriptLabs.hint: inside if x*x+y*y<=1. pi ≈ 4*inside/n. SE ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)*4; 95% CI ≈ est ± 1.96*SE.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math, random

def estimate_pi(n):
    inside = sum(1 for _ in range(n)
                 if (lambda x, y: x*x + y*y <= 1)(random.random(), random.random()))
    return 4*inside/n

for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    est = estimate_pi(n)
    p = est/4
    se = 4*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} err={abs(est-math.pi):.2e} 95%CI=({est-1.96*se:.4f},{est+1.96*se:.4f})')
# Lesson: error shrinks as 1/sqrt(N) — the Monte Carlo rate; CIs quantify it.

scriptLabs.title: Least Squares from Scratch
scriptLabs.brief: Fit y = ax + b to noisy data via the normal equations — no libraries. Then verify against the closed form. The geometry of regression, by hand.
scriptLabs.starter:
# data: noisy line
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
# TODO: solve [sum x^2, sum x; sum x, n] [a; b] = [sum x*y; sum y]  (normal equations)
# print a, b
scriptLabs.solution:
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
n = len(xs)
sx, sy = sum(xs), sum(ys)
sxx, sxy = sum(x*x for x in xs), sum(x*y for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
# normal equations: a = (n*Sxy - Sx*Sy)/(n*Sxx - Sx^2)
den = n*sxx - sx*sx
a = (n*sxy - sx*sy)/den
b = (sy - a*sx)/n
print(f'y = {a:.4f}x + {b:.4f}')  # ~ y = 2x + 0.1
# Lesson: least squares is projection — the normal equations are geometry, not magic.

scenarios.context: Variant B converts 5.2% vs A's 5.0% over 10k users each. Ship it?

options.text: Statistical significance: z-test for proportions — is 0.2pp real or noise?
options.why: 0.2pp on 10k users needs a significance test — the standard error decides, not the point estimate.
Point estimates without uncertainty are how noise ships to production.

options.text: Not significant — don't ship on this evidence; run longer or accept the null
options.why: p > 0.05: the difference is consistent with noise. Ship on evidence, not hope.
'Trending' without significance is storytelling. The test said: inconclusive.

answerBank.q: Where do I start if math is rusty?
answerBank.a: The placement diagnostic — usually Module 2 (tech math) for fluency, then the spine from college algebra. Don't start calculus with shaky algebra; the gate exists to save you months.

answerBank.q: How much math for machine learning?
answerBank.a: Linear algebra (vectors, eigenvalues, SVD), probability (Bayes, distributions, MLE), calculus (gradients, chain rule). That's Module 1's back half — the platform gates IL-07/IL-16 on these nodes.
They're a writing skill: do every exercise, read proofs actively (cover the next line, predict it), and keep a proof journal. Induction first — it's the most mechanical, and it builds the muscle.

answerBank.q: Is the electrician track only for electricians?
answerBank.a: The math (DC theory, shop math) and reading (SQ3R, code literacy) transfer to any trade. The etA credential sequence is electrician-specific; the study skills are universal.

answerBank.q: Quant math without a finance background?
answerBank.a: Yes — the module is prerequisites, not trading. Measure theory, stochastic processes, and time value of money are the language; the ladder (in IL-10's quant track) comes after.
By hand until fluent, then calculator for speed. Exams and job sites test the fluency; the tool is for after you understand.
